title: Half of what returns cost us comes from two causes we can fix: damage in transit and product photos that mislead
subtitle: A mixed-methods look at H1 2026 returns: 889k returned units, $29.4M in cost, and about $5.6M a year that three changes could save.
summary: In H1 2026, 11.0% of units shipped were returned (889k), at a cost of $29.4M. Damage in transit (31% of cost, concentrated in carton-shipped flat-pack furniture and fragile items packed on two auto-bagger lines) and 'didn't match description' (tied to missing scale shots and colour-calibrated swatches) make up about half of it. Repacking fragile SKUs, protecting or rerouting the most damage-prone furniture, and reshooting 1,200 SKUs would save about $5.6M a year, net of cost.
key_findings: Returns cost $29.4M in H1 2026 (11.0% of units, 889k); furniture is 8% of returned units but 42% of the cost.
Damage in transit is 21% of returned units but 31% of return cost; carton-shipped flat-pack furniture is damaged at 58 per 1,000 vs. 16.5 for white-glove.
Fragile items packed on the Allentown L4 and Columbus L2 auto-baggers are damaged at 92 per 1,000, 8× the rate for pulp-insert cartons.
SKUs missing a scale shot or calibrated swatch are returned as 'didn't match description' at 2.6–3.9% of units, vs. 1.4% with a full photo set.
Three actions (fragile repack, furniture protection, photo reshoots) would save ≈$5.6M a year net.
